title: Rotations: Matrices, Order, and the Angle That Vanishes

questions.question: How should you read the columns of a rotation matrix?
options: Each column is where one axis ends up
Each column is one of the three angles
Each column is a scale factor for that axis
The columns have no individual meaning
questions.explanation: That reading makes the signs checkable by hand: apply the matrix to a unit axis and you should get the corresponding column back.

questions.question: What makes a matrix a rotation rather than any other matrix?
options: Every column has length one and every pair of columns is perpendicular
Its determinant is not zero
It contains only sines and cosines
It is square
questions.explanation: Being orthonormal is exactly the statement that lengths and angles survive the transform, which is what turning something means, and it is the property drift destroys.

questions.question: Rx(90) then Ry(90) compared with Ry(90) then Rx(90):
options: They give different orientations, because rotation does not commute
They give the same orientation
They differ only in sign
The second is invalid
questions.explanation: Try it with a book. This is why every convention has to state its order, and why using a different one silently gives wrong answers everywhere.

questions.question: Why is the transpose of a rotation also its inverse?
options: Because the columns are orthonormal, which is precisely that condition
Because rotations are symmetric
Because the determinant is one
It is a coincidence that holds only for small angles
questions.explanation: It also gives a free diagnostic: if transposing no longer undoes the matrix, the matrix has stopped being a rotation.

questions.question: At pitch of ninety degrees, adding the same amount to roll and yaw changes the matrix by about 1e-16. Why?
options: The roll and yaw axes have been turned onto each other, so only their difference matters
The arithmetic overflows at that angle
Because cosine of ninety degrees is zero and the terms cancel by accident
Because the tolerance in the test is too loose
questions.explanation: Two of the three numbers have collapsed into one. It is structural: three numbers cannot cover every orientation smoothly, and no axis order avoids it.

questions.question: Why must long running code renormalise its rotation matrices?
options: Rounding accumulates until the matrix stops keeping lengths and starts scaling and shearing
Because matrices lose precision when stored
To keep the determinant positive
Because compilers reorder floating point operations
questions.explanation: The measured drift after a hundred thousand compositions is small, growing, and one directional. It never recovers on its own.
